title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Estimating Multi-Week Engagements: Beyond the 30-45 Minute Task”, what is the central focus?
options: The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution, not the unit of estimation.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution, not the unit of estimation. This lesson teaches you to size a real multi-week delivery: how to break a large engagement into estimable pieces, why you estimate the critical path and not the total, how to put the constraints and reviews from Lesson 5 into the number, and how to keep an estimate honest when the environment reveals surprises.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution.
The 30-45 minute task is not the unit of execution.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: The 30-45 minute task is the unit of execution.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
An integration delay pushes everything after it, and the pessimistic case of an early task becomes the starting condition of the next.
The opposite is true: an integration delay pushes everything after it, and the pessimistic case of an early task becomes the starting condition of the next.
questions.explanation: An integration delay pushes everything after it, and the pessimistic case of an early task becomes the starting condition of the next.

questions.question: Per the lesson about team delivery, what is the central focus?
options: A history of collaboration software
Splitting work across owners on the axes of who owns it and in what order, with the seam as a written durable contract
A review of unrelated project tools
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that splitting work is interface design, and nearly every team that fails is failing at a seam, not a part.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The seam can live in one person's memory because the team is small
Parallel subagents spawned and collected are a durable team
A seam carries what the piece delivers, what it needs, and its acceptance bar, written and durable so both sides can read it
Give every piece a dependency so nothing runs out of order
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the seam must be a written, durable thing that both sides can read, because memory lives in one head and dies with the conversation.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A maker can grade their own work because they know it best
A review noted in a status column is as good as a gate that blocks the flow
An anonymous spawned child holds a role across a delivery as well as a named profile
The orchestrator decomposes, routes, and observes, and does not execute the pieces themselves
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the orchestrator's deliverable is the shape of the team and the integrity of its seams, not any single piece of production work.

questions.question: Per the lesson about the internal pilot, what is the central focus?
options: Scoping a real slice of a prospect's problem as a bounded proof that converts into a signed engagement instead of a free spec
A history of sales enablement
A review of unrelated demo tools
A summary of pricing policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the craft of the fence that keeps a pilot from becoming a free engagement and turns it into a transaction.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A pilot is a chance to show off what the tool can do and impress the client
The pilot must prove the whole engagement so the client sees it all work
The pilot is a hypothesis test with a specific, measurable, falsifiable claim written before you build
Use clean synthetic data so the pilot always succeeds
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a pilot that converts is a hypothesis test, not a demo, and the claim names the deliverable, accuracy, time, and cost.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Set the conversion gate after the pilot succeeds so the client has seen the proof
The conversion gate is set before the pilot starts, with the scope, price, and timeline sketched in advance
A baseline can be estimated after the pilot from memory
Price the engagement from a market guess rather than the pilot's evidence
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that after the pilot the power shifts, so the gate with its terms must be agreed before it proves anything.

questions.question: Per the lesson about quality at scale, what is the central focus?
options: Keeping output correct at volume with a living golden set, binding eval gates, and regression discipline that triages failures
A history of QA software
A review of unrelated testing tools
A summary of compliance policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that volume defeats review, so you gate changes and sample the live stream instead of reading everything.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The golden set is a document you write once and lock forever
Move the expected output to match the system when a case fails, to keep the gate green
The golden set is living reference data with provenance, grown with restraint, and never edited to encode today's bug
A case with provenance is a guess that will eventually be removed
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the set exists to hold the bar, so you never move the expected output just to make the gate pass.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A failing gate with no owner is fine because the deploy deadline is real
A red gate is triaged as a real regression, stale reference, or flaky test, each with a different fix
High false alarms are harmless because the gate still protects
A gate that fires and is ignored is better than no gate because it creates awareness
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a failing gate is an event with an owner, and naming which of the three diagnoses it is is the whole skill.

questions.question: Per the lesson about cost and reliability engineering for an agent estate, what is the central focus?
options: Modeling and containing recurring spend of a fleet of agents while engineering so no single part takes the whole delivery down
A history of cloud billing
A review of unrelated monitoring tools
A summary of sales policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a running estate is a recurring cost plus a standing reliability obligation, and the levers are shared.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The weekly burn is estimated after handover so the client sees a settled number
Route the mechanical share of the fleet off the model entirely, into no-agent scripts that cost nothing and cannot drift
Run every judgment job on the most capable model at full reasoning effort for consistency
Give every job a full fallback chain regardless of how trivial the run is
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the cheapest reliable run never calls a model, so deterministic mechanical work belongs in no-agent scripts.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: When an unpinned job's global default changes, the job should silently inherit the switch so the fleet stays running
A broken job may fail quietly since a fleet has redundancy
A misconfigured job should burn tokens to prove it is broken
An unattended job should fail closed and alert rather than guess and spend, so cost control and reliability are the same mechanism
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the fails-closed posture: an unpinned job whose default changes skips, alerts, and spends no inference, protecting both budget and honesty.
